title: 1426: a case built from your youth
dramatic_question: Shāhrukh has summoned you over the verse. What do you say about it?

invariants.text: Your unswerving, impartial application of the Sharīʿa earned you enemies among Yazd's entrenched elite, who sent a delegation to Shāhrukh seeking your dismissal (your own account, in the first apology).
When the delegation failed, your enemies compiled a case from statements in works of your youth, claiming to find for example a verse praising ʿAlī and condemning ʿUmar and ʿUthmān.
invariants.detail: The witness is a later chronicler, Maʿṣūm ʿAlī Shāh, not the apology.

invariants.text: Shāhrukh summoned Ibn Turka to Herat to be tried again (reported in his own apology and in Melvin-Koushki's summary of it).
Even the staunchly Sunni Naqshbandiyya allowed praise of ʿAlī and the Imams (tawalliʾ) but not hateful condemnation of the first three caliphs and ʿĀʾisha, which was called Rāfiḍism (tabarruʾ).

prose: The delegation from Yazd asked Shāhrukh to dismiss you, and it failed. Your enemies then went through your early writings and, in the account of the later chronicler Maʿṣūm ʿAlī Shāh, claimed to find a verse praising ʿAlī and condemning ʿUmar and ʿUthmān. The chronicler is the witness; the first apology does not mention it.

Shāhrukh summons you to Herat. He is the ruler who abolished the Yasa and enforced the Sharīʿa, and the charge you answered in 1422 was Sufi bias, which Melvin-Koushki reads as probably meant to tie you to the Ḥurūfīs. If the chronicler is right, this one goes straight at your Sunni credentials. Melvin-Koushki's timeline gives the accusation of 1426 as heresy and Shiʿi proclivities. On the line that even the staunchly Sunni Naqshbandiyya drew, praising ʿAlī was allowed and condemning the first caliphs was not; a verse that condemns ʿUmar and ʿUthmān falls on the wrong side of it (our reading of that line, not a report of the trial).
The pages do not say whether you wrote the verse, or whether you owned or disowned it. What you say about it, or do not say, is what you have to decide.

choices.label: Answer the charge of Sufi bias at length, and say nothing about the verse.
costs: The verse stays in the file, unanswered.
choices.feedback: This is what the first apology does. Melvin-Koushki notes that it never mentions the verse but answers the charge of ṣūfīgarī, and that its sweeping dismissal of every position but the Sunni one clearly implies your Sunni credentials had also been questioned. The apology is your own word to the ruler judging you, so the silence is a fact about the text; what was said aloud at the hearing is not in the pages the game has read.

choices.label: Own the verse, and defend your love of ʿAlī openly as a Shāfiʿī may.
costs: Those who share your devotion to ʿAlī rally to you, and you stand on the ground of an old Sunni tradition. The accusers' charge is granted, and exposure and enemies rise.
choices.feedback: No source has him owning the verse, and the apology is silent on it. Melvin-Koushki does note that his writing on ʿAlī and the Imams fits an established Sunni tradition of praise, which is the ground this line would stand on. The game returns you to the record: the apology answers a different charge. What you gained and paid here stays in your ledger; the story then rejoins the record.

choices.label: Deny that the verse is yours, and answer the charge of Sufi bias as well.
choices.feedback: The sources do not say whether the verse was his, so this line asserts something the record cannot check. It is also not what the apology does: it says nothing about the verse at all. The game returns you to the record. What you gained and paid here stays in your ledger; the story then rejoins the record.
costs: If the denial is believed the charge loses force, so exposure falls. If the page is produced you are a liar as well as a suspect, and enemies rise. It claims what the record cannot check.

choices.label: Ask Bāysunghur to have the scholars of his court examine the charge instead.
costs: Needs Bāysunghur's favour already earned, and spends it. If his scholars clear you, the charge loses force, so exposure falls.
choices.feedback: In letter 17 you answered an objection to one of your treatises by inviting Bāysunghur to have his court's scholars examine it, so the habit is documented. No source has you doing this over the verse in 1426, and the sources put the hearing before Shāhrukh at Herat. The game returns you to the record. What you gained and paid here stays in your ledger; the story then rejoins the record.
